newsitem.title: KENYA: FOCUS-Kenyan shilling weak but small gain at close.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kenyan shilling weak but small gain at close.

text.p: Kenya's battered shilling remained weak on Tuesday despite a slight gain at the close after the World Bank said it had delayed paying part of a loan package unless Kenya addressed concerns on graft and governance.
Commercial bank dealers told Reuters that dollar inflows of up to $2 million from Tuesday's weekly coffee auction boosted the shilling mildly but failed to significantly reverse its slide.

The shilling edged up 0.62 percent to close at a commercial mean of 70.04 from the morning opening of 70.48, a new official low since July 31 when the International Monetary Fund cancelled a key aid package to Kenya citing corruption.
This latest movement brought the shilling's total loss since then to 17.71 percent.
"What we have here is a correction," a senior trader told Reuters.
Another said: "Today everyone traded cautiously because of the morning shock. Most tried to stay square."
He was referring to the shilling's new official record low at the market opening. The previous official low of 70.26 was touched on Thursday last week.
"Judging from the new information from the World Bank, we expect to see further shilling weakening," one dealer said.

Earlier commercial bank dealers had said they expected coffee inflows to cushion the shilling on Tuesday but that would be followed by further depreciation because commercial and foreign investor demand for the dollar remained very heavy.

On Monday, the shilling fell 1.64 percent from 68.87 as nervous foreign investors pulled out of the market, no longer certain about the country's economic stability after the IMF halted its three-year $205 million package on July 31.

A World Bank official in Washington, who asked not to be named, said the bank shared the concerns of the IMF, which cancelled the first year of its loan programme complaining that government was not doing enough to stamp out corruption.

"The second tranche of our structural adjustment loan had been suspended because policy conditions (on privatisation) had not been met, but we would find it difficult to release this money until the IMF programme is back on track," he said.
With Kenya's aid packages from the two institutions now in cold storage, market analysts said confidence necessary to revive the currency remained lacking.
The World Bank official said the Kenyan government had received a first tranche of the loan last year, but the second instalment, totalling just over $71 million, had not been paid.

Last week Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi, seeking to calm a nervous market, said the government was considering talks with the IMF over a second-year arrangement for the aid. But the Fund swiftly poured cold water on Mudavadi's statement making it clear there would be no talks until Kenya tackled runaway graft said by aid officials to be costing the country millions in dollars.
President Daniel arap Moi at first dismissed the significance of IMF aid to his country but later turned around and promised to fight corruption at all levels of his embattled government.
Moi is at the centre of a major battle with opposition groups calling for sweeping constitutional reforms before elections this year.
He has also had to deal with crippling industrial unrest in the last week after air traffic controllers nearly brought air traffic to its knees.

Kenya's equity and currency markets have also been hit by investor perception of political instability after violence in Nairobi and other provincial towns since May 31 when an opposition-backed pro-reform group launched a campaign for constitutional reforms before general elections.
